figures.title: Fetal heart rate decelerations
figures.caption: VEAL CHOP: Variable decelerations mean Cord compression, Early mean Head compression, Accelerations mean OK, and Late mean Placental insufficiency. Early ones need only watching; late and variable ones need action.
figures.yLabel: Heart rate traces, contraction at bottom

series.label: Contraction
series.note: Two uterine contractions. The grid lines mark each one's start, peak and end; time every deceleration against them.

series.label: Early: head compression
series.note: A mirror image of the contraction: begins, bottoms out and recovers with it. Benign; keep watching.

series.label: Late: placental insufficiency
series.note: Starts at the peak and recovers after the contraction ends. Stop oxytocin, turn to her side, give IV fluids and oxygen.

series.label: Variable: cord compression
series.note: Abrupt V-shaped drop at any time, with or without a contraction. Reposition, stop oxytocin, check for a prolapsed cord.

figures.title: Fetal heart rate baseline and variability
figures.caption: Read the baseline over 10 minutes, between contractions. Moderate variability is the most reassuring sign on the strip. A reactive nonstress test shows 2 accelerations of at least 15 beats/min lasting 15 seconds within 20 minutes.

bands.label: Bradycardia
bands.note: Below 110 for 10 minutes: cord compression or prolapse, maternal hypotension, hypoxia. Reposition, notify.

bands.label: Tachycardia
bands.note: Above 160 for 10 minutes: maternal fever or infection, fetal hypoxia, terbutaline. Check her temperature.

bands.label: Absent
bands.note: A flat line. Ominous with recurrent late or variable decelerations: intervene and notify at once.

bands.label: Minimal
bands.note: Fetal sleep, opioids or magnesium sulfate. If it lasts beyond a sleep cycle, suspect hypoxia and report.

bands.label: Moderate
bands.note: The fetus is well oxygenated right now.

bands.label: Marked
bands.note: Above 25: may be an early sign of hypoxia. Assess and report.

figures.title: Magnesium sulfate: therapeutic and toxic
figures.caption: Magnesium sulfate prevents eclamptic seizures, and toxicity shows in order: reflexes fade, breathing slows, then the heart stops. Check reflexes, respirations and urine output every hour. Calcium gluconate IV is the antidote.

bands.label: Subtherapeutic
bands.note: The normal serum level is 1.5 to 2.5; below 4 may not prevent seizures.

bands.label: Therapeutic
bands.note: About 5 to 8.4 mg/dL. Warmth, flushing and drowsiness are expected; reflexes stay present.

bands.label: Reflexes lost
bands.note: Patellar reflexes fade, then disappear: the first sign of toxicity. Stop the infusion and notify.

bands.label: Breathing fails
bands.note: Respiratory depression, then arrest. Stop the infusion, support breathing, give calcium gluconate.

bands.label: Cardiac arrest
bands.note: Heart block and cardiac arrest. Start CPR; give calcium gluconate IV.

bands.label: Too slow
bands.note: Below 12: stop the infusion, notify the provider, check reflexes and the magnesium level.

bands.label: Safe
bands.note: At least 12 a minute. Recheck every hour.

bands.label: Too low
bands.note: The kidneys clear magnesium, so it builds up. Notify the provider before it reaches toxic levels.

bands.label: Adequate
bands.note: At least 30 mL/hr, measured hourly through an indwelling catheter.

figures.title: Preeclampsia and its severe features
figures.caption: Birth is the only cure. Headache, vision changes and epigastric pain are warning signs to report at once. Watch for HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) and eclamptic seizures.
rows: Blood pressure
140/90 or higher twice, 4 hours apart, after 20 weeks
Systolic 160 or higher, or diastolic 110 or higher
Protein in urine
Usually 300 mg or more in 24 hours
Not needed when severe features are present
Brain and eyes
No symptoms
Severe headache that medication doesn't relieve; blurred vision or spots
Liver
Normal
Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain; liver enzymes twice normal
Platelets and kidneys
Normal
Platelets below 100,000; creatinine above 1.1 or doubled
Lungs
Clear
Pulmonary edema
Nursing care
BP and fetal checks; teach warning signs to report
Magnesium sulfate, IV labetalol or hydralazine, seizure precautions

figures.title: Postpartum hemorrhage: first actions
figures.caption: A pad soaked within 15 minutes, a rising pulse and a boggy fundus mean hemorrhage; the pulse climbs before the blood pressure falls. A firm fundus with a steady trickle of bright red blood points to a laceration instead.

steps.title: Massage the fundus
steps.detail: Support the lower uterus with one hand and massage the fundus with the other until it firms. A boggy uterus (atony) causes most early bleeding.

steps.title: Empty the bladder
steps.detail: A full bladder pushes the uterus up and to one side so it can't contract. Help her void, or catheterize if she can't.

steps.title: Call for help and stay
steps.detail: Use the call light to summon the provider or rapid response team. Keep massaging, and weigh pads: 1 g is about 1 mL of blood.

steps.title: Give uterotonics as prescribed
steps.detail: Oxytocin first. No methylergonovine with hypertension or preeclampsia; no carboprost with asthma. Misoprostol is another option.

steps.title: Replace volume
steps.detail: Large-bore IV access, rapid IV fluids, then blood products. Give oxygen, check vitals every 5 to 15 minutes, and measure urine output hourly.

figures.title: Lochia after birth
figures.caption: Lochia goes from red to pink-brown to white and should never go backward. A steady trickle of bright red blood with a firm fundus is not lochia: suspect a laceration.
rows: Rubra
Days 1 to 3: dark red, a few small clots
Clots the size of an egg or larger
Serosa
Days 4 to 10: pinkish brown and thinner
It turns bright red again
Alba
Day 10 to about 6 weeks: yellowish white
Red bleeding returns, or it lasts well past 6 weeks
Amount
Scant to moderate; a gush on first standing up is normal
A pad soaked in an hour or less
Odor
Fleshy, like a menstrual period
Foul smell, fever or a tender uterus: suspect endometritis

figures.title: Stages of labor
figures.caption: Events, not the urge to push, mark the stages: the second stage starts at full dilation (10 cm) and ends with the birth. The fourth stage, the first hours after the placenta delivers, is when hemorrhage risk peaks.
rows: First stage: latent
Regular contractions begin; cervix dilates to about 6 cm
Walking, fluids and comfort; teach breathing techniques
First stage: active
About 6 cm to full dilation (10 cm); contractions every 2 to 3 minutes
Monitor fetal heart rate and contractions; pain relief; void every 2 hours
Transition
8 to 10 cm: strongest contractions, shaking, nausea, rectal pressure
Stay with her; pant-blow breathing; no pushing before full dilation
Second stage
Full dilation (10 cm) until the baby is born
Coach pushing with contractions; watch the fetal heart rate closely
Third stage
Birth of the baby until the placenta delivers, usually within 30 minutes
Signs of separation: a gush of blood, the cord lengthens, the uterus rises
Fourth stage
First 1 to 2 hours after the placenta delivers
Fundus, lochia and vitals every 15 minutes for the first hour; bleeding risk peaks

figures.title: Newborn normal values
figures.caption: Values for a term newborn at rest. Cold stress, low glucose and breathing trouble feed each other, so a finding in one means checking the others. Glucose cutoffs vary by nursery protocol.

bands.label: Bradycardia
bands.note: Report now. At birth, a rate below 100 calls for positive-pressure ventilation.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Brief dips in deep sleep can be normal. Recheck while awake.

bands.label: Normal
bands.note: Up to about 180 while crying.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Sustained at rest: check the temperature; think sepsis or respiratory distress.

bands.label: Low
bands.note: Check for cold, low glucose or maternal opioids. Pauses of 20 seconds or more are apnea.

bands.label: Normal
bands.note: Irregular, abdominal breathing with brief pauses is normal.

bands.label: Tachypnea
bands.note: Sustained, or with grunting, flaring or retractions: respiratory distress. Report.

bands.label: Cold stress
bands.note: Burns glucose and oxygen. Skin-to-skin, dry the baby, add a hat, or use a radiant warmer.

bands.label: High
bands.note: Check for overbundling. 38 C (100.4 F) or higher needs a sepsis evaluation.

bands.label: Hypoglycemia
bands.note: Jittery, weak cry, poor feeding. Feed, recheck in 30 to 60 minutes; IV dextrose if still low.

bands.label: Acceptable
bands.note: Screen infants of diabetic mothers and large, small or preterm newborns in the first hours.

figures.title: Pediatric vital signs by age
figures.caption: Approximate ranges for a calm, awake child; sources differ by a few beats. The younger the child, the faster the rates. Crying, fever and pain raise them, and bradycardia in a sick child is an ominous late sign.
rows: Newborn (first month)
Infant (1 to 12 months)
Toddler (1 to 3 years)
Preschool (3 to 6 years)
School-age (6 to 12 years)
Adolescent (over 12 years)

figures.title: Developmental milestones
figures.caption: Ages are typical, not deadlines, and preterm infants are judged by their corrected age. Refer any child who loses a skill already gained, has no steady head control by 6 months, or can't sit alone by 9 months.
rows: 2 months
Lifts head when on the stomach
Social smile; coos
4 months
Holds head steady; rolls front to back; reaches for toys
Laughs aloud; turns toward voices
6 months
Rolls back to front; sits with support; passes toys hand to hand
Babbles consonants (ba, da); stranger anxiety begins
9 months
Sits alone steadily; crawls; pulls to stand
Object permanence (peekaboo); separation anxiety
12 months
Cruises along furniture, may take first steps; neat pincer grasp
1 or 2 words with meaning; waves bye-bye
18 months
Walks well, climbs; stacks 3 or 4 blocks; uses a spoon
About 10 to 20 words; points to body parts
2 years
Runs, kicks a ball, walks up stairs
2-word phrases, 50 or more words; parallel play
3 to 4 years
Rides a tricycle; hops on one foot by 4; copies a circle
Sentences strangers understand; plays with other children

figures.title: Dehydration in infants and children
figures.caption: Weight loss sets the grade: 1 kg lost is about 1 liter of fluid. Use oral rehydration solution, not juice, soda or plain water. Aim for urine output of at least 1 mL/kg/hr, and add potassium to IV fluids only after the child voids.
rows: Mild (3 to 5% weight loss)
Alert; slightly dry lips; normal pulse; slightly less urine
Oral rehydration solution in small, frequent sips; keep feeding
Moderate (6 to 9%)
Irritable; dry mouth; few tears; fast pulse; sunken fontanel; refill 2 to 4 seconds
Oral rehydration solution, about 5 mL every few minutes; IV if vomiting prevents it
Severe (10% or more)
Lethargic; no tears; rapid weak pulse; cool mottled skin; little or no urine
Emergency: IV normal saline bolus of 20 mL/kg, repeated as needed

figures.title: Croup vs epiglottitis
figures.caption: Epiglottitis is an airway emergency. Never examine the throat or swab it, never lay the child down, and never leave; keep intubation and tracheostomy equipment at the bedside.
rows: Cause
Virus, most often parainfluenza
Bacteria, classically H. influenzae type b
Typical age
6 months to 3 years
2 to 5 years; older if not vaccinated
Onset
Gradual, after a cold; worse at night
Sudden, over a few hours
Hallmarks
Barking, seal-like cough; hoarse voice; stridor
Drooling, trouble swallowing, muffled voice, no cough; tripod position
Fever
Low grade
High; the child looks toxic and anxious
Care
Cool mist; oral steroid; nebulized epinephrine for stridor at rest
Keep calm and upright; no throat exam; ready for intubation; IV antibiotics

figures.title: Is breastfeeding going well?
figures.caption: Output shows intake. A tender lump without fever is a plugged duct: feed often and massage toward the nipple. With mastitis, keep breastfeeding or pumping, rest, drink fluids and finish the antibiotic.
rows: Latch
Wide mouth, lips turned out, much of the areola inside, audible swallows
Pain past the first minute, clicking, a creased nipple after feeds
Feedings
8 to 12 in 24 hours, started on early cues such as rooting
Fewer than 8 a day, or a newborn too sleepy to feed
Wet diapers
About one per day of age at first; 6 or more a day by day 5
Fewer than 6 a day after day 5, or dark urine
Stools
3 or more yellow, seedy stools a day by day 5
Still passing dark meconium after day 4
Weight
Loses up to 7% in the first days; back to birth weight by 10 to 14 days
More than 7% lost: assess the feeding; 10% or more: notify
Breasts
Full, firm and tender on days 3 to 5: feed often to relieve it
A hard, red, hot wedge with fever and aches: mastitis

figures.title: Pyloric stenosis vs intussusception
figures.caption: Pyloric stenosis vomit is never bilious and the infant stays hungry; intussusception brings bouts of pain and currant jelly stool. Hirschsprung disease differs again: no meconium in the first 48 hours, then ribbon-like stools.
rows: Typical age
Usually 3 to 6 weeks old
Usually 3 months to 3 years
Hallmark
Projectile, nonbilious vomiting right after feeds; hungry again at once
Sudden colicky pain: screams and draws knees to chest, calm between bouts
Stools
Fewer and smaller
Red, mucus-filled currant jelly stool (a later sign)
Exam
Olive-shaped mass in the upper abdomen; visible stomach waves
Sausage-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen
Main danger
Dehydration, low potassium and chloride, metabolic alkalosis
Bowel ischemia, perforation and shock
Treatment
Correct fluids and salts first, then surgery to split the pyloric muscle
Air or contrast enema reduces it; surgery if that fails
Report
Signs of dehydration: fewer wet diapers, sunken fontanel
A normal brown stool: the bowel may have reduced on its own

figures.title: Childhood rashes
figures.caption: Match the rash to the story. Varicella and measles spread through the air; fifth disease is contagious only before the rash; rubella and parvovirus both endanger a pregnancy. Never give aspirin to a child with a viral illness.
rows: Measles (rubeola)
Cough, runny nose, red eyes, Koplik spots; blotchy rash from face down
Airborne; very contagious. Report to public health
Rubella
Mild illness; pink rash face to trunk; swollen nodes behind the ears
Droplet; keep away from anyone pregnant (birth defects)
Varicella
Itchy crops of spots, blisters and crusts all at once
Airborne and contact until every lesion crusts; no aspirin
Fifth disease
Slapped-cheek face, then a lacy rash on the arms and legs
Contagious only before the rash; can harm a fetus
Roseola
3 to 5 days of high fever, then a pink rash as the fever breaks
Febrile seizures can occur during the fever
Scarlet fever
Sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue after strep throat
Finish all the penicillin; contagious until 24 hours of antibiotics
Hand, foot and mouth
Painful mouth sores; blisters on hands, feet and diaper area
Handwashing; the virus stays in stool for weeks; push fluids
Impetigo
Honey-colored crusts around the nose and mouth
Contact spread; school after 24 hours of antibiotics
